title: The Philippines as Part of the World
subtitle: Where your country sits, and why that position decided its history.
objectives: Describe the absolute and relative location of the Philippines
Name the three main island groups and locate them
Identify the seas and countries that surround the Philippines
Explain how being an archipelago shapes life and travel
Explain how location put the Philippines on world trade routes

cards.title: Your country has coordinates
cards.text: The Philippines sits in Southeast Asia, on the western edge of the Pacific Ocean. Almost everything about its history comes from that one fact.

cards.title: You already know how coordinates work
cards.text: Minecraft gives you X, Y and Z. Earth gives you latitude and longitude. Same idea, older system.
points: **Latitude** = how far north or south. Like Z.
**Longitude** = how far east or west. Like X.
**Two numbers pin any point on the planet.**
**Nobody needs a landmark** if they have the numbers.

cards.title: The exact numbers
cards.text: Absolute location is the coordinates. It never changes and it doesn't depend on anything else.
points: **Latitude: about 4°N to 21°N.**
**Longitude: about 116°E to 127°E.**
**All north of the equator, all east of the Prime Meridian.**
**Being close to the equator** is why it's hot all year.

cards.title: The other way to say where you are
cards.text: Relative location describes a place by what's around it. It's how people actually talk.
points: **"South of Taiwan, east of Vietnam."** That's relative.
**"14°N, 121°E."** That's absolute.
**Both are correct.** They answer different questions.

question.text: Which of these is an ABSOLUTE location?
question.explain: The coordinates. The others all describe the Philippines by what's around it, which makes them relative.

cards.title: Tap the island groups and the seas
cards.text: Three island groups, the waters on each side, and the neighbours. Two quiz questions come from this map.

cards.title: An archipelago of 7,641 islands
cards.text: The Philippines isn't one landmass. It's thousands of islands, and only about 2,000 of them have people living on them.
points: **Luzon** in the north — the largest, and the capital.
**The Visayas** in the middle — a scatter of islands.
**Mindanao** in the south — the second largest.
**The official count rose to 7,641** in 2016 after new surveys.

question.text: Put the three island groups in order, from north to south.
question.explain: Luzon north, Visayas in the middle, Mindanao south. It's the single most useful thing to know about the map.

cards.title: Surrounded on every side
cards.text: The Philippines shares no land border with any country. Everything arrives by sea or air.
points: **East:** the Philippine Sea, open Pacific.
**West:** the West Philippine Sea.
**South:** the Celebes Sea.
**North:** the Luzon Strait, then Taiwan.

cards.title: No land border changes everything
cards.text: You can drive from France to China. You cannot drive out of the Philippines at all.
points: **Ferries and planes do the work** roads do elsewhere.
**Between islands**, a ferry is the bus.
**Goods arrive by ship**, which is why ports matter so much.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: You've got the map. Part 2 is why this position mattered to the rest of the world. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Sitting on the route everyone wanted
cards.text: The Philippines lies between mainland Asia and the Pacific. For centuries, that made it a place ships passed through — and then a place they stopped.

cards.title: A crossroads before it was a country
cards.text: Long before Spain arrived, traders from China, India and across Southeast Asia were already coming.
points: **Chinese porcelain and silk** arrived by sea.
**Islam reached Mindanao** through trade routes from the south.
**Goods, religions and words** travelled the same paths.
**Position, not size**, is what made it matter.

cards.title: The same position brought Spain
cards.text: Magellan reached the islands in 1521 while looking for a westward route to the Spice Islands. The Philippines was on the way.
points: **Spain ruled for over 300 years.**
**The country is named after King Philip II** of Spain.
**Manila became the Pacific end** of a trade route to Mexico.
**That route ran for 250 years.**

question.text: Why did the Philippines become important to traders and colonisers?
options: Its position on the sea routes between Asia and the Pacific
It was the largest country in Asia
It had the biggest population in the region
It was the only place with fresh water
question.explain: Location, not size. It sat on the route between mainland Asia and the Pacific, so ships passed through it.

cards.title: Typhoons and the Ring of Fire
cards.text: The same location that brought trade also brings the weather and the earthquakes.
points: **Typhoons form over the warm Pacific** and travel west into the islands.
**Around twenty a year** enter Philippine waters.
**It sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire**, so earthquakes and volcanoes are common.
**Same position. Both consequences.**

cards.title: You can see all of this from orbit
cards.text: From the ISS the archipelago is unmistakable — a scatter of green between two very different blues.
points: **Typhoons are visible as spirals** moving west across the Pacific.
**Satellites track them days ahead**, which is why warnings work.
**Being near the equator** also makes it useful for launching satellites.

cards.title: Still defined by the map
cards.text: The Philippines is part of ASEAN and the United Nations, and its position still shapes its relationships.
points: **ASEAN** links it to its Southeast Asian neighbours.
**Its time zone is UTC+8**, shared with China and Singapore.
**Disputes in the West Philippine Sea** are about that same position.

question.text: The Philippines shares a land border with Malaysia.
question.explain: False. It shares no land border with any country. Every neighbour is across water, which is why sea travel matters so much.

cards.text: The Philippine Trench, east of Mindanao, is over 10,000 metres deep. Drop Mount Everest into it and the peak would still be more than a kilometre underwater.

terms.def: A country or region made up of many islands.
An exact position given as latitude and longitude.
A position described by what is around it.
How far north or south of the equator a place is.
How far east or west of the Prime Meridian a place is.
The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, at 0° latitude.
The belt around the Pacific where most earthquakes and volcanoes occur.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Absolute** = coordinates. **Relative** = what's around it.
**Three groups, north to south:** Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao.
**7,641 islands and no land border.** Everything arrives by sea or air.
**Position brought the trade** — and the typhoons.

quiz.text: Put the three main island groups in order from north to south.
quiz.explain: Luzon in the north with the capital, the Visayas scattered through the middle, Mindanao in the south.
quiz.objective: Name the three main island groups and locate them

quiz.text: Which is an example of ABSOLUTE location?
quiz.explain: Coordinates are absolute. Everything else describes the Philippines by reference to something nearby, which is relative.
quiz.objective: Describe the absolute and relative location of the Philippines

quiz.text: What word describes a country made up of many islands?
quiz.explain: An archipelago. The Philippines has 7,641 islands, of which around 2,000 are inhabited.
quiz.objective: Explain how being an archipelago shapes life and travel

quiz.text: The Philippines shares a land border with at least one other country.
quiz.explain: False. It has no land border at all. Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia and Palau are all across water.
quiz.objective: Identify the seas and countries that surround the Philippines

quiz.text: Which sea lies to the EAST of the Philippines?
quiz.explain: The Philippine Sea, open Pacific. The West Philippine Sea is on the other side, to the west.
quiz.objective: Identify the seas and countries that surround the Philippines

quiz.text: Why did the Philippines end up on world trade routes?
options: It lay between mainland Asia and the Pacific
It was the richest country in Asia
It had the largest ports already built
It was the only land in the region
quiz.explain: Position. Ships travelling between Asia and the Pacific passed through, so traders stopped — and later, so did colonisers.
quiz.objective: Explain how location put the Philippines on world trade routes

quiz.text: Roughly how many islands does the Philippines have?
quiz.explain: 7,641 as of the 2016 survey, up from the long-quoted 7,107. Only around 2,000 are inhabited.
quiz.objective: Explain how being an archipelago shapes life and travel

quiz.text: The Philippines lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so earthquakes and volcanoes are common.
quiz.explain: True. The same Pacific position that brought trade also brings the earthquakes, the volcanoes and around twenty typhoons a year.
quiz.objective: Explain how location put the Philippines on world trade routes

quiz.text: Which island group contains the capital, Manila?
quiz.explain: Luzon, the largest island and the northern group. Roughly half the country's population lives there.
quiz.objective: Name the three main island groups and locate them

options: How far north or south of the equator a place is
How far east or west a place is
How high above sea level a place is
How far from the nearest ocean a place is
quiz.explain: North–south. Longitude is the east–west one. Two numbers together pin any point on Earth.
quiz.objective: Describe the absolute and relative location of the Philippines

quiz.text: Being an archipelago with no land border means that…
options: Almost everything and everyone arrives by sea or air
The country cannot trade with anyone
The islands all share one language
quiz.explain: Ferries and planes do the work roads do elsewhere, and ports matter enormously. It also helps explain the number of languages.
quiz.objective: Explain how being an archipelago shapes life and travel

quiz.text: Relative location means describing a place using its exact coordinates.
quiz.explain: False — that's absolute location. Relative location describes a place by what's around it, like 'south of Taiwan'.
quiz.objective: Describe the absolute and relative location of the Philippines

teacher.summary: Week 1 Social Studies covers the Philippines as part of the world, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is organised around a single argument — that position explains the country's trade history, its colonisation, its weather and its present-day disputes — rather than as a list of facts to memorise. The interactive map reuses the explorer component from the Science lessons, so no new interface has to be learned. The map is deliberately schematic; it teaches relative position and the island groups, not coastline detail.
discussion: Ask him to give both an absolute and a relative location for your own town. Doing both for one place makes the distinction stick.
Ask why the Philippines has so many languages. The archipelago structure is most of the answer, and he can reason his way there.
Ask what the Philippines and Japan have in common. Both are archipelagos on the Ring of Fire, and both were shaped by sea trade.
Ask what would be different if the Philippines had a land border with China. It tests whether he understood why the water matters.
teacher.extension: Have him mark the three island groups and the four surrounding seas on a blank map from memory, then add one arrow showing the direction typhoons arrive from. It combines the location facts with the consequence in a single diagram.
misconceptions: 'The Philippines is one island.' It is an archipelago of 7,641 islands in three main groups.
'Absolute and relative location are the same.' Absolute is coordinates and never changes. Relative depends on what you compare it to.
'The Philippines borders Malaysia by land.' It has no land border with anyone. Every neighbour is across water.
'The country was named after a Filipino leader.' It was named after King Philip II of Spain.
